syllabusTopics: Limits and continuity: limits of a function, indeterminate forms, algebraic properties of limits (without proof), basic theorems on limits of algebraic, trigonometric, exponential and logarithmic functions
Continuity of a function, types of discontinuity, graphs of discontinuous function
Derivatives: derivative of a function, derivatives of algebraic, trigonometric, inverse trigonometric, exponential and logarithmic functions by definition (simple forms)
Rules of differentiation; derivatives of parametric and implicit functions; higher order derivatives
Geometric interpretation of derivative; monotonicity of a function, interval of monotonicity, extreme values of a function, concavity, points of inflection
Anti-derivatives: integration using basic integrals, integration by substitution and by parts methods
The definite integral; the definite integral as an area under the given curve; area between two curves

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Continuity: f continuous at c iff lim_{x→c}f(x) = f(c). Types of discontinuity: removable, jump, infinite.  ·  Every discontinuity of a function falls into one of four categories: removable, jump, infinite, or essential.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: A removable discontinuity can be "fixed" by redefining the function at one point. Jump and infinite discontinuities cannot be removed this way.  ·  The function $f(x) = \sin(1/x)$ for $x \neq 0$ and $f(0) = 0$ has an essential discontinuity at $x = 0$ — no matter how you define $f(0)$, the limit does not exist.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Understanding discontinuities is crucial for integration — a function with a finite number of removable or jump discontinuities can still be integrated.  ·  Continuity is essential for the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, which connects derivatives and integrals.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **Fact.** Continuity: f continuous at c iff lim_{x→c}f(x) = f(c). Types of discontinuity: removable, jump, infinite.  ·  **Removable discontinuity (hole):** The limit $\lim_{x \to a} f(x)$ exists, but either $f(a)$ is undefined or $f(a) \neq \lim_{x \to a} f(x)$. The graph has a "hole" at $x = a$. Example: $f(x) = \frac{x^2 - 1}{x - 1}$ at $x = 1$.  ·  **Jump discontinuity:** The left-hand and right-hand limits both exist but are not equal: $\lim_{x \to a^-} f(x) \neq \lim_{x \to a^+} f(x)$. The graph "jumps" at $x = a$. Example: the floor function $f(x) = \lfloor x \rfloor$ at every integer.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: A vertical asymptote always indicates an infinite discontinuity, but not all discontinuities involve vertical asymptotes.  ·  A function can be continuous at a point but not differentiable there (e.g., $f(x) = |x|$ at $x = 0$). Continuity is a weaker condition than differentiability.  ·  A function can have a limit at a point without being continuous there — the function might be undefined at that point, or its value might differ from the limit.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: one worked example for "Continuity of a function, types of discontinuity, graphs …" — check units / edge cases.  ·  recall card: definition → formula → limit → one error to avoid.  ·  Classify the discontinuity of $f(x) = \frac{x^2 - 4}{x - 2}$ at $x = 2$.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Sketch the graph of $f(x) = \begin{cases} x + 1 & x < 0 \\ x^2 & x \geq 0 \end{cases}$ and classify any discontinuities.  ·  For $f(x) = \frac{1}{x - 3}$, identify the type of discontinuity at $x = 3$ and describe the behaviour from both sides.  ·  Determine whether $f(x) = \begin{cases} x^2 & x \neq 1 \\ 3 & x = 1 \end{cases}$ is continuous at $x = 1$.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Find the value of $k$ that makes $f(x) = \begin{cases} kx + 1 & x \leq 2 \\ x^2 & x > 2 \end{cases}$ continuous at $x = 2$.  ·  Use the Intermediate Value Theorem to show that $x^3 - x - 1 = 0$ has a root in $[1, 2]$.  ·  The Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees the existence of solutions to equations but does not tell you how to find them.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: State the limit / condition where a formula or rule stops being valid before applying it.  ·  Limit to remember: indeterminate forms 0/0, ∞/∞, 0·∞ → l'hôpital: lim f/g = lim f'/g' (when applicable).  ·  **Infinite discontinuity (asymptotic):** At least one of the one-sided limits is $\pm \infty$. The graph has a vertical asymptote at $x = a$. Example: $f(x) = 1/x$ at $x = 0$.
